Question: What happened to the Dutch settlers on the east coast of what is now the USA?
Answer: Peter Stuyvesant, the pegleg fellow in the middle, surrenders New Amsterdam to the forces of the Duke of York. New Netherlands included communities in what are now New York, New Jersey, Delaware, and Connecticut. English forces seized them in 1664. The terms negotiated for New Amsterdam (now New York) and environs were extremely generous, basically promising that no one would be disturbed, freedom of religion was guaranteed, the pubs would stay open, etc. Peter Stuyvesant, the one-legged Dutch governor, had little choice but to accept them. The terms said anyone who wanted to go home to Holland could do so, and anybody who wanted to go to England could do that, too, at the expense of the English. What a deal! I take it Pete and his boys went home, and the Dutch folks who had homes and farms probably stayed, unless they had some other reason to leave. A separate English force seized the Dutch settlements further south, in what is now Delaware, and treated the people harshly. But the transfer of New York was accomplished without bloodshed or trauma.

Question: Wh architects designed the Key Bridge and why do these photos make it look like they put absolutely no thought whatsoever into the possibility of collisions with out-of-control ships? https://www.shutterstock.com/search/francis-scott-key-bridge?
Answer: The Francis Scott Key Bridge in Baltimore was designed in 1971–1972 by the J.E. Greiner Co., a civil engineering company in Baltimore that specialized in bridge design. (The company was acquired by another firm in 1995.) Construction of the bridge began in 1972 and it was opened to traffic in 1977. The bridge itself was 1.6 miles long. The picture can’t really do it justice — that thing was humongous. The roadway was 185 feet above the water. The bridge was fine for its time, but the state transportation department kind of ignored the fact that the ships going under it were getting bigger and bigger. Containerships back then were maybe 600 feet long and carried 2,000 containers. The MV DALI that hit the bridge was almost 1,000 feet long and carried 20,000 containers. She displaced almost 100,000 ton EMPTY. She may have displaced 140,000 tons when loaded — creating a gigantic amount of force if it hit anything. Other bridge owners have scrambled to protect their property from these mammoth ships. The Sunshine Skyway bridge over Tampa Bay in Florida had to be rebuilt after a ship strike in 1980. The state installed “dolphins,” or huge concrete bumpers, to try to ward off errant ships. Other bridge owners are doing the same. It’s also smart to protect the “piers,” or vertical supports, of a bridge by setting them in massive stone islands. These defensive structures take up room in the ship channel, however, leaving less room for the ships to travel. For that reason, I’m guessing the Baltimore bridge will be replaced with a suspension bridge which has a longer span, leaving more room for the islands and dolphins.

Question: During the American Civil War, did any groups of civilians ever band together to help the Union fight and battle the Confederate army?
Answer: Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. John L. Burns, the "old hero of Gettysburg," with musket and crutches, July 1863 (Library of Congress). John Burns was 69 years old and a veteran of the War of 1812 when the Confederates invaded his home town of Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, in July 1863. He grabbed his old flintlock musket and went out to help the Union soldiers fight the rebels in Herbst Woods. The amazed young soldiers told him to get out of there, but apparently he spent some time blasting away at the enemy. He survived the battle and met President Lincoln during his visit in November. Well-meaning civilians were not welcome on the front lines, where they would just get in the way and spread panic when the shooting started. However, civilians did valuable work behind the lines. The Sanitary Commission was a private group that helped with soldiers’ health and well-being. “Sutlers” were merchants who followed the armies and sold canned goods, fruits and vegetables, and other treats. The militia were civilians with military training to one level or another. They didn’t play much of a role after the early days of the war but could be called out in an emergency. Harrisburg, the capital of Pennsylvania, was swarming with militia during the Gettysburg campaign. They didn’t get into the fight to any noticeable degree, though. And civilians did take up arms in the internecine fighting in contested areas like Missouri and the frontier. Irregular warfare is even more hellish than organized war. War is hell.

Incomes are also lower, and it’s just a fact of life that poorer people tend to have more health problems, for a wide variety of reasons. Overweight and obesity overall in Mississippi is actually pretty similar to national prevalence, although diabetes is somewhat more prevalent. On the bright side, Mississippians are less likely to have a drinking problem than Americans nationwide, and considerably fewer automobile fatalities are caused by drunk driving in Mississippi than nationwide. Question: Why did the confederacy invade northern territory in 1862 instead of fortifying their borders and remaining on the defensive?
Answer: Robert E. Lee, left, was an offensive strategist until forced onto the defensive; Joseph E. Johnston, top, was cautious and attacked only when needed; John Bell Hood was reckless on offense. Robert E. Lee was always interested in moving the war out of Virginia. By late summer 1862, he was probably thinking of shoving the Union forces back so that Virginia farmers, particular in the bountiful Shenandoah Valley, could harvest their crops in peace. He also knew that Maryland was full of Confederate sympathizers and may have seen the state as a source of support for the rebel cause. Lee was also a soldier of the old school and probably hoped to bring the Union army to a decisive battle, an Austerlitz or Waterloo. Antietam was more of a draw, however, and certainly not a decisive victory. Finally, Lee agreed with the maxim that you can do anything you like with a sword except sit on it. He had defeated the Yankees twice — the Seven Days and Second Manassas — and saw no reason to stop. That courtly demeanor masked a very aggressive fighting spirit. The Army of Northern Virginia was on the offensive until the end of the day July 3, 1863. As for defending the borders — the South could not possibly stand on the defensive. The Union had too many places to break through. Lee was finally forced into a defensive strategy after Gettysburg, beginning with the battle of the Wilderness in the spring of 1864, and he did the best he could, but the Confederacy collapsed just a year later. At least Lee had rivers as defensive barriers. In the West, the rivers were avenues of invasion for the Federals. The South simply couldn’t stop them. The Confederacy really had no chance to win the war, but that’s hindsight. Looking at the situation at the time, Lee felt that only an aggressive approach could win. The Confederates took a more defensive strategy in the West, but that led to the disaster at Vicksburg. The only aggressive Confederate commander in the West was John B. Hood, who mistook reckless tactics for a strategy. That ended in disaster, too. In the end, Joe Johnston said all he could do was “annoy the Yankees.” The Union was just too strong.
